items.excerpt: Erin L. Cox argues that as publishers chase new revenue from licensing works to train LLMs, microdeals and other complex rights arrangements, opaque royalty reporting stops being tolerable. Real-time visibility into sales and payment data becomes the precondition for author trust in AI licensing.

Spotify is testing three AI-driven audiobook discovery features: a prompt-based playlist generator, natural-language search that answers questions about a book's content across formats, and improved series tracking. It reframes book discovery as a conversational interface rather than a browse-and-filter catalog.

Dr Alan Finkel, Australia's former chief scientist and founder of Proudly Human, warns that AI delivers "no economic benefits for the arts or the creative sector" and pushes for stronger structural protections for creators against AI-generated content.

Dale L. Roberts' self-publishing news roundup on how the EU AI Act's transparency rules are reaching indie authors worldwide — including what AI-content labelling and disclosure now mean for writers publishing outside Europe.

Frankfurt Rights explains why AI licensing requests still have to be negotiated one by one — use, scope, remuneration, reporting and liability differ too much for a standardized workflow — and says the platform has hardened security after sustained attacks from AI bots scraping rights listings.
